chunks: Steady state at minimum and maximum current. The question: Describe what happens to a motor/solenoid at steady-state under minimum and maximum current draw?.
"Steady state" means the motor has settled and nothing is still changing. In that state, how much current a motor draws depends on how fast its shaft is turning.
Held still (stalled), it draws the most current. Spinning freely with no load, it draws the least.
Picture a hose filling a tank from the bottom. The water level in the tank pushes back against the hose. With an empty tank, water rushes in.
As the level rises, the flow slows to a trickle. A spinning motor makes its own "level", called back-EMF, that rises with speed and pushes back against the supply.
The analogy breaks down in one place: the motor builds that push by spinning, so a stalled motor has none.
At the left (stall) the red copper-loss curve equals the input, so all 144 watts is heat.
Moving right, the back-EMF absorbs more of the input and the blue mechanical output rises, peaking at 36 watts at 300 rad/s (half the free speed), then falls to zero at the ideal speed.
The ratio of blue to grey is the efficiency: 50% at the power peak, higher still beyond it.
Steady state: everything has settled, so the current is no longer changing. Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates that opposes the supply.
Stall: the shaft is held still, so speed is zero. No-load: the shaft spins freely and nothing but friction slows it. Winding: the motor's coil of copper wire.
Its resistance, in ohms (Ω), limits the current at stall. Inductor: a coil that resists changes in current. Once the current stops changing, it drops no voltage.
Use a 12 volts supply and a motor winding of 1 ohms. Stalled, there is no back-EMF, so the current is 12 volts / 1 ohms = 12 amps .
The power is 12 volts times 12 amps = 144 watts, and all of it becomes heat. Spinning freely, suppose the back-EMF reaches 11. 5 volts. Only 0.
5 volts is left across the winding, so the current is 0. 5 amps . That is the whole idea: more speed means more back-EMF, which means less current.
"At steady state the inductor drops nothing, so the winding is its resistance plus back-EMF.

At maximum current the motor is stalled: no back-EMF, I equals V over R, maximum torque, and all the input power V squared over R, 144 watts in my 12 volts, 1 ohm example, becomes winding heat, so it burns out in seconds.
At minimum current it's free-running: back-EMF nearly equals the supply, current is just friction, about half an amp, and the power goes into friction and windage.
A solenoid's steady state is always V over R unless you reduce the voltage."
